PreMRA: Predictive multi-object resource allocation
framework based on unsupervised deep learning for
process optimization
Abstract—Predictive process-aware systems enable organiza-
tions to anticipate the evolution of running processes and proac-
tively adjust operational decisions based on real-time process
changes. In this context, resource allocation becomes one of
the critical factors influencing end-to-end process performance,
as different allocation strategies can lead to vastly different
cycle times, operational costs, and service outcomes under the
same control flow structure. However, existing resource alloca-
tion methods typically rely on manual rules, complex process
modeling, and problem-specific feature engineering, which limit
their adaptability across different process traces and make it
difficult to automatically learn multi-objective trade-offs under
practical execution constraints. To address these challenges, this
study proposes a predictive multi-objective resource allocation
framework based on unsupervised deep learning. It first predicts
the complete control flow of the ongoing trace, and then generates
a relatively optimal resource configuration in real time. In the op-
timization phase, we reformulate multiple performance objectives
into a unified unsupervised loss function and optimize the alloca-
tion scheme through backpropagation. It allows decision-makers
to flexibly adjust preferences between different performance
metrics by tuning loss weights. Furthermore, we also design
two resource allocation generation strategies to accommodate
different flexibility requirements in process execution. Extensive
experiments conducted on seven synthetic datasets built upon
real-world event logs demonstrate that the proposed method
consistently generates improved and robust resource allocation
schemes across different business scenarios and execution traces.
Index Terms—Resource allocation, Multi-object, Process opti-
mization, Unsupervised deep learning, Predictive process moni-
toring
I. INTRODUCTION
B
USINESS process optimization has become one of the
key pathways to improve organizational competitiveness
in the context of digital transformation and intelligent op-
erations
cite kumar2002dynamic, kumar2020business, pu-
fahl2025resource. Business process performance depends not
only on the rationality of the control flow but also signifi-
cantly on the resource perspective [1], [2], i.e., who performs
which activity at what time. In practical scenarios, changes
in resource allocation strategies can lead to the same process
model exhibiting vastly different cycle times, operating costs,
and service experiences under different resource allocation
strategies. Therefore, resource allocation is not a secondary
configuration of process execution, but rather a core decision-
making link that determines end-to-end process performance.
In an environment characterized by fluctuating demand, re-
source constraints, and service commitments, systematically
optimizing resource allocation has direct economic value and
management significance [3]–[5].
Resource allocation optimization aims to select appropriate
execution resources for activity instances within a process,
given a set of resources and business constraints, and to
determine their allocation timing and priority to achieve prede-
fined performance objectives [4], [6], [7]. The significance is
reflected in multiple aspects, such as reducing waiting times to
shorten cycle times and improve service levels [8], controlling
or lowering operating costs by increasing resource utilization
[6], [7], and improving overall service quality and customer
experience by balancing multiple objectives [1], [5].
Existing research has explored various approaches to re-
source allocation optimization [1]. Resource allocation meth-
ods based on process execution data typically focus on
statistical data or execution rules from historical execution
logs, demonstrating the value of historical execution data for
resource allocation optimization [5], [8]–[13]. These studies
often rely on rule mining algorithms or optimization strategy
design, making it difficult to provide adaptive resource alloca-
tion solutions for different execution traces [1]. Furthermore,
resource allocation methods based on process models usually
rely on complex modeling work and optimization rule design,
and are solved through mathematical programming [8], [9],
[14]–[16], heuristic search [2], [17]–[19], or reinforcement
learning [20], [21]. These methods focus on the process model
structure while neglecting the characteristics of historical exe-
cution data, which may lead to optimization results that deviate
from actual execution constraints. Although these methods
have shown good optimization results in experiments, they
struggle to automatically capture multi-objective trade-offs
in complex scenarios [1], [4]. Given these limitations, we
aim to develop a data-driven method that can automatically
learn multi-objective trade-off mechanisms and constraint rules
for resource allocation from historical execution data without
relying on specific problem-specific rule design, and maintain
robustness across different execution paths.
In addition, resource allocation optimization is dynamic and
context-dependent [1], [4], [20], [21]. The optimal strategy
for the same type of task may differ depending on its posi-
tion within the process structure. This requires optimization
methods that can characterize complex state dependencies
and possess adaptive capabilities. Therefore, when allocat-
ing resources, it is crucial to fully utilize process-related
data and pay attention to the dynamic changes in business
processes. Fortunately, predictive process-aware information
systems (PAIS) provide the ability to monitor and predict
complete business processes in real time [22], [23]. By lever-
aging predictive business process monitoring methods, the
system can predict upcoming business traces, thereby pro-

## Page 2

IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SERVICES COMPUTING
2
viding proactive execution information for resource allocation
optimization.
In this study, we propose a predictive resource allocation
optimization framework (PreMRA) that can capture business
process changes in real time and provide optimal business
resource configurations. To this end, for the resource allocation
problem of a single process, we designed an adaptive multi-
objective optimization method based on unsupervised deep
learning. Specifically, we simultaneously considered process
execution information from historical event logs and the pro-
cess model structure, and used a convolutional neural network
to learn the hidden features. Then, we transformed multiple
optimization objectives into an unsupervised learning loss
function and used a backpropagation mechanism to optimize
the resource allocation scheme. This method allows us to
adjust our preferences for different process performance in-
dicators by tuning the parameters of the loss function. Finally,
we proposed two resource allocation generation strategies to
meet the execution flexibility preferences of different decision-
makers. Furthermore, we constructed seven synthetic datasets
based on real event logs for evaluation. Experimental re-
sults show that the proposed resource allocation optimiza-
tion method can effectively learn the features of historical
execution data and process models, providing better resource
allocation schemes for different process traces across multiple
datasets. In summary, the main contributions of this study are
as follows:
1) We develop a predictive resource allocation framework
for process optimization, enabling resource configura-
tion decisions based on real-time process changes.
2) We propose a multi-objective resource allocation opti-
mization method based on unsupervised deep learning,
which can automatically learn constraints from historical
execution data and process structures.
3) We designed two resource allocation generation strate-
gies to accommodate decision-makers’ preferences re-
garding the flexibility of process execution.
4) We evaluated the effectiveness and robustness of the
proposed method using seven synthetic datasets across
different business scenarios and execution traces.
The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section
II presents a review of the relevant literature. Section III
introduces several basic concepts and the graph convolu-
tional network. Section IV introduces the framework of the
proposed predictive resource allocation approach for process
optimization and Section V details the multi-objective resource
allocation optimization method based on unsupervised deep
learning. In Section VI, we present extensive experimental
results on the proposed optimization method. Finally, Section
VII presents the study conclusion and possible future research
directions.
II. RELATED WORKS
As a key technology for improving the efficiency of en-
terprise business processes, resource allocation has received
widespread attention in the industry [1], [3]. Optimizing
resource allocation needs to be based on the actual process
structure or historical process execution data to meet practical
production requirements [1], [6], [7]. Based on the different
forms of data used, existing research is mainly divided into
two categories: process execution-based methods and process
model-based methods.
A. Process execution-based methods
Early studies applied association rule mining algorithms
to hospital and enterprise workflow logs to discover fre-
quently occurring activity-resource combinations and derive
resource allocation rules or candidate resource recommen-
dation schemes [8], [9]. These methods utilize simple co-
occurrence patterns and lift-based filtering methods, but they
are limited to static rules, relying on manually specified
constraints and thresholds, making them difficult to adapt to
constantly changing process conditions or multiple conflict-
ing objectives [8], [9]. Furthermore, some studies focus on
measuring and utilizing resource behavior from event data.
They use process mining techniques to quantify resource pref-
erences and collaboration patterns for organizational analysis
and process redesign [5], [24]. Although these methods can
capture important behavioral aspects, they primarily provide
descriptive insights or a limited catalog of allocation patterns
and cannot directly learn allocation strategies that optimize
performance under complex constraints.
Other research focuses on building optimization models
based on execution logs to improve process performance
through better resource allocation. For example, allocation
models that consider time and collaboration factors can min-
imize process completion time under preferences, cost con-
straints, and availability criteria, or reduce cycle time by
minimizing worklist entropy and balancing workloads, thus ef-
fectively utilizing task similarity and collaboration information
[12], [13]. Other studies combine historical execution obstacles
or stochastic simulations with metaheuristic algorithms (such
as differential evolution algorithms) to find near-optimal hu-
man resource allocation schemes under uncertainty [10], [25].
These methods demonstrate that log-based optimization can
improve throughput and robustness, but they typically target
only a single or very limited objective and rely on manually
designed features and simulation assumptions. More recently,
predictive business process monitoring has been combined
with scheduling optimization to support proactive resource
allocation. Such methods first use machine learning models to
predict future process behavior and then solve an optimization
problem (e.g., minimizing total weighted completion time),
thus demonstrating the value of combining prediction with
allocation decisions [11].
Overall, existing process execution–based methods rely on
shallow models, rule mining, or handcrafted simulation and
optimization pipelines, and they rarely address simultaneous
optimization of multiple performance dimensions such as time,
cost, and service quality, which motivates the development
of our deep learning–based multi-objective resource allocation
framework.

## Page 3

IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SERVICES COMPUTING
3
B. Process-model based methods
Process model-based resource allocation methods typically
start with an explicit process representation (e.g., Petri nets
and BPMN) and then optimize allocation under the modeled
constraints. First, several studies model work assignment as
a sequential decision problem and learn adaptive allocation
strategies through reinforcement learning [20], [21]. However,
such methods are attractive for handling dynamic conditions,
as they often rely on high-quality feedback mechanisms and
may incur high training costs. Second, several studies treat
resource allocation as a scheduling problem embedded in the
process control flow. For example, [14] combines the Hungar-
ian algorithm with analytical or simulation components and
heuristic search to obtain optimal or near-optimal task-resource
scheduling under a fixed process model. Other studies employ
metaheuristics or mathematical programming methods, includ-
ing genetic algorithms [17], dynamic reallocation methods
based on queueing theory and stochastic theory [15], improved
hybrid particle swarm optimization methods [18], and mixed-
integer programming combined with heuristic methods [16].
These methods are generally more interpretable than purely
learning-based methods and can provide effective solutions in
well-defined environments, but they rely on careful objective
and constraint design, and they often face scalability and
robustness issues when process execution uncertainty is high.
Furthermore, encoding an expressive subset of BPMN using
rewriting logic allows for the definition of executable formal
semantics, thereby supporting simulation-based analysis of
resource usage and allocation decisions [26]. [27] proposed
a formal method for BPMN with quantitative annotations,
enabling the automatic comparison of dynamic resource al-
location strategies based on recent usage, recent requests, or
predictions.
Although existing research has made significant progress,
most process-based methods still rely on extensive modeling
work and manually designed optimization objectives, and they
are not designed to learn directly from large amounts of
heterogeneous execution data. Given these limitations, our
goal is to develop a data-driven approach that can automat-
ically capture complex, multi-objective trade-offs in resource
allocation without relying on problem-specific rule design.
Therefore, this study addresses the process resource allocation
problem for a single process and proposes an unsupervised
deep learning-based adaptive optimization method. Facing
multiple optimization objectives, the proposed method can
provide adaptive resource allocation optimization solutions for
different business traces within the same business scenario.
Our method considers not only historical process execution
information but also process model structural features, and
experimental results demonstrate that this helps improve the
optimization performance.

IV. OVERALL FRAMEWORK
The overall framework of PreMRA is shown in Figure 2.
It is divided into three main phases to accomplish real-time
process prediction and resource allocation optimization. In
the first phase, the PAIS captures business execution records
and updates the business process model. In the second phase,
the predictive model learns from event logs and related
process model information to predict the complete control
flow structure of the running trace. In the resource allocation
optimization phase, on the one hand, a neural network is used
to learn from event logs and related process model information
to build a resource allocation optimization model. On the
other hand, based on the control flow of the predictive trace
provided in the data recording phase, the optimization model
provides an adaptive resource allocation scheme. This resource
allocation scheme is then used to guide process managers in
controlling and managing the execution of the running trace.
Finally, after the current trace is completed, the execution
trace is recorded in the event log by PAIS. The system checks
whether the process model has changed; if it has, the predictive
model and the optimization model are updated.
The methods for the second phase have been extensively
studied, and many excellent approaches are available in the
existing literature [22], [23], [31]. Therefore, this study mainly
focuses on the resource allocation optimization phase and
proposes a deep learning-based multi-object resource allo-
cation method for process optimization. For ease of under-
standing, we formulate this problem as follows. Given an
event log L, we create a dataset Q for optimization model
training and comparing, represented as {(σi, Ci)|1 ≤i ≤|L|}.
Here, (σi, Ci) denotes a pair of “trace-resource allocation”
collection, which means that the resource allocation for σi
is Ci. The ultimate goal of process optimization is to improve
the efficiency of business processes, which typically involves
reducing operating time and costs, increasing the flexibility of

participation matrices. We set the log-level activity relationship
and resource participation matrices as binary matrices, while
the trace-level ones depend on the number of events and the

relationship matrix Qb indicates whether the activity sequence

value in Qi is set to 0. The trace-level resource participation
matrix Pi has the same shape as Pb, but its value represents the
number of times a specific resource is scheduled to complete
a specific activity.
Finally, we utilize Qb and Pb for node feature representation

matrix Qb reflects the node features of a particular activity in
the business scenario, while each row of matrix Pb reflects
the distribution of allocable resources for a specific activity.
Furthermore, Qi and Pi are utilized to express process con-
straints in the optimization mechanism (We will discuss this
in detail in Section V-C).
B. GCN-based learning model
To fully utilize the hidden information in event logs for
resource allocation, we developed a GCN-based deep learning
model to learn deep features of traces (See Figure 4). As
a neural network framework specifically designed for graph
learning, GCNs take graph node features and adjacency matri-
ces as input and outperform other methods in graph structure
modeling and feature extraction [28]. Therefore, to enhance
the ability to understand the business processes of GCNs, it
is necessary to fully utilize the available information from
the event log, including the activity sequence information and
the structural information of DFGs in the process resource
allocation task.
The row vectors of Qb represent the interaction relationships
between an activity and other activities, while the row vectors
of Pb represent the configurable relationships between all
resources and a specific activity. These two aspects of infor-

understand the business scenario, we combine the two aspects

adopt a soft attention mechanism to weight the row vectors of

with Top-N selection strategy(PreMRA-NW). We evaluated

ratio (AOR), which is the proportion of traces in the test
set that are optimized; (2) average optimization magnitude
(AOM), which is the average optimization magnitude of the
performance of all traces in the test set; and (3) average
optimization time (AOT), which is the average time taken to

the PreMRA optimization method adopts the TOP-N selection

default that all performance indicators have equal importance,

3) Training setup: When performing the experiments, we
adopted the commonly used experimental setup scheme in the
deep learning field. The traces in a dataset were divided into
training sets and testing sets in a ratio of 80%: 20%. Then, a
threefold cross-validation method was adopted for the training
process. Based on the loss performance of the validation set,
we used the early stopping method to determine the optimal
network parameters. Training was stopped if the validation
loss did not decrease during 10 epochs after reaching the
maximum. We adopted the tree-structured Parzen estimator
approach [22], [23] for automatic parameter tuning, and the
parameter settings are shown in Table II. The source code was
based on the PyTorch 2.1.0 version in Python 3.9.13, and all
experiments were conducted on a GPU platform with NVIDIA
GeForce RTX 4090.
B. Results
1) Comparison results: Table III reports the performance
of different methods on AOR. The proposed method achieves
better resource allocation optimization results in terms of
process cost and process execution time. Furthermore, in terms
of overall performance, the proposed method provides better
resource allocation for over 70% of the execution traces across
most datasets. Table IV reports the performance of different
methods on AOM. Compared to all baseline methods, the
proposed method provides significant improvements in both
performance metrics and overall performance. Specifically, for
the execution traces in the Helpdesk dataset, it reduces costs
by an average of 27.85% and execution time by 61.59%. Table
V reports the time taken by different prediction methods. All
methods took approximately 0.001 seconds to configure re-

method in practical operation.

method outperforms PreMRA-NP and PreMRA-NQ in most
cases, demonstrating that considering both the structural char-
acteristics of the process model and process execution infor-

networks. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the TOP-
N strategy generally outperforms the Top-one strategy. This
indicates that neural network predictions do not always accu-
rately identify the optimal activity-resource combination.

3) Performance indicator correlation analysis: According
to [6] and [7], in real-world business scenarios, the mul-
tiple performance dimensions of business processes can be
conflicting. Improvements are typically measured across four
dimensions, corresponding to the standard metrics of cost,
time, flexibility, and quality found in the literature. To achieve
higher quality results, one might expect to incur higher costs
and spend more time. These conflicting objectives are con-
sidered to form a devil’s quadrangle [6], [7], as shown in
Figure 10. The dashed quadrilateral in the diagram shows
the modified metrics of a redesigned process as part of a
process improvement exercise, where time savings may come
at the cost of higher costs and reduced flexibility. Therefore, in
this section, we aim to investigate whether the PreMRA opti-
mization method can provide robust results when performance
metrics are conflicting by changing the correlation between
cost and time performance.
We first generate random execution times (between 0 and
1) for each activity-resource group. Then, for each activity-
resource combination, we generate the execution cost using
the following formula:
Cost = ϑ × (1 −Time) + (1 −ϑ) × ζ
(11)
Where ϑ is the correlation coefficient between the two per-
formance indicators, a larger ϑ indicates a greater conflict
between the two indicators. ζ represents a random noise,
which is used to reduce the functional relationship between
the two metrics, making the generated results more natural.
Two performance indicators, ϑ, and ζ are between 0 and 1.
Figures 8 and 9 show the performance of the PreMRA
optimization method under different correlation levels, where
the horizontal axis represents the correlation coefficient. Ac-
cording to Figure 8, as the correlation coefficient (ϑ) in-
creases, the optimization rate of the trace in terms of both
execution cost and time gradually decreases. As shown in
Figure 9, with the increase of ϑ, the AOM of the trace
gradually approaches 0 across all metrics. In summary, the
results indicate that the increasing conflict between cost and
time affects the optimization performance of the PreMRA
optimization method. Therefore, when there are conflicting
objectives in optimizing process resource allocation, we need
to make trade-offs between different objectives to achieve
the best optimization quality [6], [7]. For example, process
managers can adjust their preferences based on the conclusions
in Section 5.3.2 to obtain a resource allocation that better
meets expectations.

optimization framework that can capture business process
changes in real time and generate optimal resource config-
urations. To address the resource allocation problem within
a single process, we developed an adaptive multi-objective
optimization method based on unsupervised deep learning.

jectives as an unsupervised learning loss function and optimize
the allocation scheme through backpropagation. This design

To evaluate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed
method, we generated seven synthetic datasets based on real
event logs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed
method achieves better resource allocation optimization results
in terms of process cost and process execution time. The
proposed method provides better resource allocation schemes
in over 70% of execution traces across multiple datasets. In
terms of execution efficiency, the proposed method requires
only about 0.001 seconds of resources per trace, reflecting
its high efficiency in practical applications. Second, compared
with baseline methods, it was found that considering both the
structural characteristics of the process model and process exe-
cution information can improve the optimization performance
of the neural network. Third, further experiments demonstrate
that the proposed method can provide personalized resource al-
location optimization schemes based on different performance
objective preferences. Finally, we also evaluated the robustness
of the proposed method when there are conflicts in different
process performance indicators.
Although the proposed PreMRA framework brings new in-
sights to resource allocation, it still has some limitations. First,
the dynamism and sustainability of our resource allocation
optimization depend on the prediction results of the predictive
monitoring model. Errors in the prediction model will propa-
gate to the resource allocation optimization stage. Therefore,
future work needs to focus on reducing the propagation of

these errors. Furthermore, this study focuses on the resource
allocation optimization problem for a single trace. However,
the same employee may be responsible for performing dif-
ferent tasks in multiple traces simultaneously. Future work
will explore using unsupervised deep learning to solve the
resource allocation optimization problem in scenarios with
multiple parallel traces and perform batch solving. Finally,
the optimization model’s training is based on historical data,
making it difficult to cope with the impact of concept drift
in business processes. Therefore, future work needs to design
environment-aware and feedback mechanisms to enable the
algorithm to adapt to changes in process structure.
